constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Distributed retrieval in classroom learning
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Using at least two of the independently authored synthetic source summaries, develop a qualified claim about whether high school courses should include brief, low-stakes retrieval opportunities distributed across the week when the goal is durable learning.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus:
SYNTHETIC EVIDENCE SET FOR PRACTICE — THESE ARE NOT REAL OR PUBLISHED STUDIES.

Source A: Eighteen introductory-psychology classes in six public high schools were assigned by class to one of two four-week routines. Retrieval classes completed three brief closed-note questions twice per week and then received corrective feedback. Comparison classes spent the same time rereading matched summaries. On a common delayed assessment four weeks later, the retrieval classes averaged 81% and the comparison classes averaged 74%. Because classes rather than students were assigned, teacher and class differences may remain.

Source B: Ninety-six adolescents learned two matched sets of unfamiliar word pairs in a laboratory. Each participant used spaced retrieval with feedback for one set and equal-time restudy for the other; set order and condition were counterbalanced. One week later, mean recall was 68% for the retrieval set and 54% for the restudied set. The artificial word-pair task may not represent complex course learning.

Source C: In a survey of 1,200 high school students, reported frequency of self-quizzing correlated positively with end-of-term course grades (r = .24). The survey did not fully control prior achievement, study time, course difficulty, or motivation, and self-reports may be inaccurate.
taskParts: A. State a defensible, qualified claim that answers the question.
B. Use one specific result from one source as evidence and explain why it supports or limits the claim.
C. Use a specific result from a different source and a relevant AP Psychology concept to justify the claim, while acknowledging an important limitation or alternative explanation.

planningFrame.label: Claim
planningFrame.guidance: Answer the policy question with conditions rather than claiming retrieval always works for every student or task.

planningFrame.label: First evidence chain
planningFrame.guidance: Select a quantitative result, identify the design, and explain how the result bears on durable learning.

planningFrame.label: Second evidence chain
planningFrame.guidance: Use a different source and connect its result to retrieval practice, spacing, feedback, encoding, or access to long-term memory.

planningFrame.label: Boundary check
planningFrame.guidance: Preserve design limits such as clustered assignment, laboratory artificiality, self-report, confounding, and modest correlation.

successCriteria: Makes a relevant, qualified claim rather than restating the question.
Uses specific evidence from at least two different synthetic sources.
Explains how each cited result supports or limits the claim rather than merely listing numbers.
Accurately applies a psychological concept and acknowledges what the evidence cannot establish.
commonPitfalls: Treating the survey correlation in Source C as proof that self-quizzing caused higher grades.
Ignoring that Source A assigned intact classes and may retain teacher or classroom differences.
Generalizing Source B's word-pair task to every kind of complex learning without qualification.
Inventing an official rubric, point total, AP score, or statistical result not included in the summaries.
sampleOutline: Claim: recommend brief, feedback-supported retrieval as one evidence-informed routine, while monitoring task fit and access.
Evidence 1: use the delayed classroom means from Source A and preserve the cluster-design limitation.
Evidence 2: use the within-person one-week recall difference from Source B and connect it to retrieval practice or spacing.
Boundary: Source C is consistent with the claim but cannot remove motivation, prior-achievement, or self-report alternatives.
constructedResponseWorkshops.reviewNote: Unscored independent planning practice using three wholly synthetic study summaries. Not official College Board sources, a prompt, rubric, point award, score, score prediction, college-credit prediction, or classroom mandate. Independent AP Psychology, accessibility, rights, and psychometric validation remain pending.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulusNature: Three independently authored synthetic study summaries; they do not describe real or peer-reviewed publications.

contentMigration.note: All native AP Psychology sections use structured lesson blocks and remain subject-expert pending.

glossary.definition: The proportion of observed variation in a trait across a specific population attributable to genetic differences rather than environmental differences; it describes population variance, not the genetic percentage within a single individual.

A brief, all-or-none electrical impulse conducted down an axon when depolarization crosses threshold, opening voltage-gated sodium channels and prompting neurotransmitter release from axon terminals into the synaptic cleft.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Neural communication, nervous systems, and the brain

glossary.definition: Chemical agents that alter synaptic transmission: agonists mimic or amplify a neurotransmitter at receptor sites, whereas antagonists bind to receptors to block or diminish the neurotransmitter signal.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Neural communication, nervous systems, and the brain

glossary.definition: The nervous system's ability to reorganize synaptic connections and functional brain pathways in response to learning, experience, or injury; plasticity is highest in early childhood but continues throughout adulthood.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Neural communication, nervous systems, and the brain

glossary.definition: The conversion of physical environmental stimuli, such as light wavelengths, sound waves, or odorant molecules, into graded receptor potentials and neural impulses transmitted along sensory pathways to the brain.

Perceptual interpretation guided by existing schemas, expectations, prior knowledge, and surrounding context, contrasting with bottom-up processing that constructs perception directly from raw incoming sensory features.

A cognitive shortcut in which people judge the frequency or probability of an event by how quickly vivid, emotional, or recent examples come to mind, often distorting estimates of true statistical risk.

A lasting increase in synaptic strength following repeated high-frequency stimulation of neural pathways, widely considered a foundational cellular mechanism supporting learning and long-term memory consolidation.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Memory as encoding, storage, retrieval, and reconstruction

glossary.definition: A memory distortion in which exposure to misleading post-event details alters a person's recollection of the original episode, demonstrating that episodic retrieval is reconstructive rather than a literal recording.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Memory as encoding, storage, retrieval, and reconstruction

glossary.definition: The degree to which a psychological assessment accurately measures the theoretical trait or cognitive ability it claims to evaluate, distinct from reliability, which reflects consistency of scores across administrations.

Systematic differences between age groups in a cross-sectional study produced by shared historical, educational, or generational experiences rather than genuine developmental maturation across the lifespan.
Associative learning in which a neutral stimulus repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus capable of eliciting an involuntary, learned conditioned response.
A learning process in which the frequency of a voluntary behavior increases when followed by positive or negative reinforcement and decreases when followed by positive or negative punishment.

The acquisition of new behaviors, skills, or outcome expectations by watching a model act and observing vicarious consequences, without requiring direct personal reinforcement during initial learning.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Observational, cognitive, and biological factors in learning

glossary.definition: Knowledge acquired through exploration without immediate external reinforcement that remains unexpressed in performance until an incentive motivates the organism to use its internal cognitive map.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Observational, cognitive, and biological factors in learning

glossary.definition: The observer tendency to overestimate internal dispositional traits and underestimate external situational pressures when explaining the causes of another person's behavior.

Unpleasant psychological tension triggered when a person holds contradictory beliefs or acts inconsistently with an attitude, motivating attitude revision, rationalization, or behavior change to restore consistency.

Impaired collective decision-making in cohesive groups where desire for harmony and unanimity overrides critical evaluation of alternatives, suppresses dissenting views, and promotes unrealistic optimism.
Bandura's social-cognitive principle holding that personal cognitive factors, overt behaviors, and environmental conditions continuously and bidirectionally interact to shape personality and action.

An individual's belief in their capacity to organize and execute the actions required to accomplish a specific task, strongly influencing goal selection, persistence, effort, and recovery after setbacks.

A stress-management strategy directed at actively altering or removing the source of a stressor through planning, skill acquisition, or direct action, generally most effective when the stressor is controllable.

An integrative health and clinical framework explaining psychological disorders and physical well-being through the interacting influences of biological predispositions, psychological processes, and social-cultural contexts.

The concurrent occurrence of two or more distinct psychological or medical disorders in the same individual, which complicates differential assessment, clinical prognosis, and coordinated treatment planning.

A structured, evidence-based psychotherapy that helps clients identify and restructure distorted thought patterns while practicing targeted behavioral skills and exposures to reduce distress and impairment.

An ethical safeguard requiring that research participants or therapy clients receive clear disclosures about procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality limits, and withdrawal rights before voluntarily agreeing.

quickReference.title: Neurobiology, Brain Systems, Sleep & Sensation
quickReference.purpose: Anchors neural firing, neurotransmitter drug action, cortical/subcortical localization, sleep architecture, and sensory transduction models in Unit 1.
checklist: Trace whether a symptom involves peripheral autonomic arousal (sympathetic vs. parasympathetic) or a specific central brain structure.
Distinguish chemical agonist action (mimics/enhances neurotransmitter or blocks reuptake) from antagonist action (blocks receptors or inhibits release).
Separate physical stimulus transduction (sensation) from cognitive interpretation (perception) when diagnosing visual or auditory phenomena.
formulas: Action potential sequence: resting potential (~ −70 mV) → threshold depolarization (Na+ rushes in, all-or-none) → repolarization (K+ exits) → refractory period; myelin speeds saltatory conduction.

Key neurotransmitters: ACh (muscle/memory), dopamine (reward/movement), serotonin (mood/sleep), GABA (main inhibitory), glutamate (main excitatory), norepinephrine (alertness), endorphins (pain relief).

Brain localization & imaging: medulla (vital functions), cerebellum (coordination), amygdala (fear/emotion), hippocampus (explicit memory consolidation), prefrontal cortex (executive control); fMRI tracks blood-oxygen activity while EEG tracks electrical timing.

Sensory theories: Weber's law (just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion); vision (trichromatic RGB cones + opponent-process afterimages); audition (place theory for high pitches, frequency/volley for low pitches); gate-control theory of pain.
decisionRules: When you see a split-brain patient shown an image solely in the left visual field → predict the right hemisphere processes it, so the patient cannot verbally name it (left Broca's area) but can pick it up with the left hand.
When you see a drug blocking serotonin reuptake transporters (like an SSRI) → classify it as a functional agonist because more serotonin stays active in the synaptic cleft.
When you see rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, high EEG brain activity, and skeletal muscle paralysis → identify REM (paradoxical) sleep rather than NREM-3 delta slow-wave sleep.
When you see a heritability statistic of 0.70 for a trait → interpret it as 70% of the variation across a population attributable to genetics, not 70% of one individual's trait.
cautions: Neurons fire with identical peak voltage regardless of stimulus intensity (all-or-none law); stronger stimuli increase firing frequency and recruit more neurons.
Damage to the hippocampus impairs forming NEW explicit memories (anterograde amnesia) without erasing old childhood memories or procedural motor skills.
Broca's area (left frontal lobe) governs speech production, whereas Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) governs language comprehension.

quickReference.title: Perception, Memory Systems, Heuristics & Psychometrics
quickReference.purpose: Connects perceptual organization, working and long-term memory mechanics, cognitive biases, and intelligence test validity/reliability.
checklist: Check whether a memory failure occurred at encoding (attention), storage (consolidation), or retrieval (cue mismatch/interference).
Distinguish whether old information blocks new recall (proactive interference) or new learning disrupts old memories (retroactive interference).
Identify whether a measurement critique targets consistency (reliability) or accuracy in measuring the intended construct (validity).
formulas: Processing & perception: bottom-up (data-driven features) vs. top-down (schemas/expectations); Gestalt grouping (proximity, similarity, closure, figure-ground); binocular retinal disparity vs. monocular depth cues.

Memory architecture: Baddeley's working memory (central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad); explicit LTM (episodic events, semantic facts) vs. implicit LTM (procedural skills, priming).

Decision heuristics & obstacles: availability heuristic (vivid/recent examples), representativeness heuristic (prototype matching), confirmation bias, framing effect, mental set, and functional fixedness.

Psychometrics: Spearman's g, fluid (novel reasoning) vs. crystallized (accumulated knowledge) intelligence; standardization norms, test-retest/split-half reliability, construct/predictive validity, and Flynn effect.
decisionRules: When you see someone overestimate shark-attack risk right after watching dramatic news coverage → identify the availability heuristic.
When you see a student who learned Spanish last year accidentally using Spanish vocabulary during a new French quiz → diagnose proactive interference (old disrupts new).
When you see an eyewitness incorporate misleading post-event phrasing ("smashed" vs. "hit") into their recall → identify Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation effect (memory reconsolidation distortion).
When you see a bathroom scale consistently reading 5 pounds too heavy every morning → classify it as high reliability but low validity.
cautions: Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment, and similarly, semantic encoding (deep meaning) outperforms shallow phonemic or structural maintenance rehearsal.
Primacy effect reflects transfer into long-term memory, whereas recency effect reflects items still active in working memory (and disappears after a delay).
A test can be reliable without being valid, but it cannot be valid without first being reliable.

quickReference.title: Lifespan Development, Conditioning & Social Learning
quickReference.purpose: Integrates developmental stage frameworks and research designs with classical conditioning, operant schedules, and observational learning.
checklist: Check whether the learning scenario involves an involuntary reflex paired with a neutral cue (classical) or a voluntary behavior shaped by its consequence (operant).
For operant items, ask two separate questions: does the behavior increase (reinforcement) or decrease (punishment), and is a stimulus added (positive) or removed (negative)?
Match developmental milestones to Piagetian cognitive operations versus Eriksonian psychosocial crises.
formulas: Developmental designs & frameworks: longitudinal (tracks same cohort over time, costly/attrition) vs. cross-sectional (compares ages at once, cohort-effect risk); Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems.

Cognitive & social development: Piaget (sensorimotor/object permanence → preoperational/egocentrism → concrete operational/conservation → formal operational/abstract); Vygotsky ZPD & scaffolding; Ainsworth attachment & Baumrind authoritative vs. authoritarian/permissive parenting.

Classical conditioning: UCS → UCR; pairing NS + UCS yields CS → CR; key phenomena include acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, stimulus generalization/discrimination, and Garcia biological taste aversion.

Operant schedules: fixed-ratio (scallop pause-run), variable-ratio (highest steady rate, most resistant to extinction), fixed-interval (scalloped ramp near deadline), variable-interval (slow steady rate).
decisionRules: When you see a driver buckling a seatbelt to stop an annoying dashboard chime → classify as negative reinforcement (removing an aversive stimulus increases buckling).
When you see a child pouring water into a taller thin glass and insisting it now holds more liquid → place the child in Piaget's preoperational stage (lacking conservation).
When you see slot-machine play persisting despite long losing streaks → identify a variable-ratio schedule producing high resistance to extinction.
When you see rats navigating a maze without reward and suddenly running it rapidly once food appears → identify Tolman's latent learning via cognitive maps.
cautions: In operant conditioning, "positive" means ADDING a stimulus and "negative" means REMOVING a stimulus—never "good" or "bad."
Authoritative parenting (high warmth + clear, reasoned boundaries) is distinct from authoritarian parenting (low warmth + rigid obedience).
Cross-sectional studies cannot separate true aging effects from generational cohort differences.

quickReference.title: Social Influence, Attributions, Personality & Motivation
quickReference.purpose: Clarifies attribution errors, conformity and group dynamics, personality frameworks, and core motivational and emotional theories.
checklist: Identify whether an attribution explains another person's mistake (fundamental attribution error) versus one's own success/failure (self-serving bias).
Check whether group presence involves individual evaluated performance (social facilitation) or pooled unidentifiable effort (social loafing).
Verify which personality perspective (psychodynamic, humanistic, social-cognitive, or Big Five trait) matches the prompt's mechanism.
formulas: Attributions & persuasion: fundamental attribution error (overweighting dispositional traits for others), actor-observer bias, cognitive dissonance (attitude shifts to match behavior), central (logic) vs. peripheral (cues) persuasion.

Group & compliance dynamics: Asch conformity (normative vs. informational influence), Milgram obedience, group polarization, groupthink (harmony overrides critique), bystander effect (diffusion of responsibility), foot-in-the-door vs. door-in-the-face.

Personality theories: Big Five OCEAN (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism); Bandura reciprocal determinism & self-efficacy; Rogers unconditional positive regard; Freud defense mechanisms.

Motivation & emotion: Yerkes-Dodson law (moderate arousal optimal; lower for complex tasks, higher for simple tasks), intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation (overjustification effect), Lewin approach-avoidance conflicts, facial-feedback hypothesis.
decisionRules: When you see a like-minded committee end a discussion holding a more extreme stance than members started with → identify group polarization (distinct from groupthink's suppression of dissent).
When you see someone agree to put a giant billboard in their yard after first agreeing to a small window sticker → identify the foot-in-the-door compliance technique.
When you see an expert musician play faster in front of an audience while a novice stumbles → identify social facilitation (audience boosts dominant well-learned responses).
When you see children stop drawing for fun once external prizes for drawing are removed → diagnose the overjustification effect undermining intrinsic motivation.
cautions: Do not confuse prejudice (an unjustified attitude), stereotype (a generalized belief), and discrimination (unjust behavior toward a group).
Negative reinforcement is behavioral, whereas cognitive dissonance requires internal psychological tension between conflicting beliefs and actions.
High scores on Big Five neuroticism indicate emotional instability/reactivity, not clinical neurosis.

quickReference.title: Stress, Positive Psych, Disorders & Evidence-Based Care
quickReference.purpose: Links stress physiology, DSM-5-TR diagnostic frameworks, psychological and biomedical treatments, and experimental evaluation of treatment efficacy.
checklist: Evaluate symptoms through the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress lenses rather than attributing disorders to a single biological or environmental cause.
Distinguish positive symptoms of schizophrenia (added experiences like hallucinations/delusions) from negative symptoms (diminished speech, flat affect, avolition).
Check experimental rigor (random assignment, double-blind placebo control, operational definitions) when judging whether a therapy study supports causation.
formulas: Stress & positive psychology: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion); problem-focused vs. emotion-focused coping; positive psychology (resilience, signature strengths, gratitude, posttraumatic growth).

Diagnostic framework (DSM-5-TR): dysfunction, distress, and deviance from cultural norms; major categories include neurodevelopmental, schizophrenia spectrum, depressive/bipolar, anxiety/OCD/PTSD, dissociative, eating, and personality disorders.

Psychotherapies: CBT (reframes maladaptive thoughts + behavioral activation), exposure/systematic desensitization (counterconditioning for phobias), client-centered humanistic (empathy, active listening), psychodynamic (insight).

Biomedical interventions: SSRIs (prolong serotonin for depression/anxiety), antipsychotics (block dopamine D2 receptors), anxiolytics (enhance GABA inhibition), lithium (mood stabilizer for bipolar), ECT/TMS for treatment-resistant depression.
decisionRules: When you see a patient pairing progressive muscle relaxation with a gradual hierarchy of feared stimuli → identify systematic desensitization (behavioral counterconditioning).

When you see a client alternating between weeks of severe hopeless depression and episodes of sleepless, euphoric, impulsive grandiosity → diagnose bipolar disorder rather than major depressive disorder.
When you see intrusive unwanted obsessions temporarily relieved by repetitive ritualistic behaviors → identify obsessive-compulsive disorder maintained via negative reinforcement.
When you see a clinical trial using random assignment to CBT vs. waitlist control and double-blind outcome raters → conclude causal evidence of treatment efficacy while controlling experimenter bias.
cautions: In schizophrenia, "positive" symptoms mean ADDED abnormal behaviors (hallucinations, delusions), NOT beneficial symptoms; "negative" symptoms mean ABSENT normal functions (flat affect, avolition).
Dissociative identity disorder (two or more distinct identity states) is completely separate from schizophrenia (psychosis/split from reality).
Correlational studies of stress and illness cannot establish causation because of third-variable confounds and bidirectional relationships.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Correlation vs. Causation and Third-Variable Blindness
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners treat a strong correlation coefficient (such as r = −0.84) as causal proof, confuse negative correlation direction with weak strength, or ignore unmeasured third variables and reverse directionality.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Inspect study design before strength: read |r| for magnitude and its sign strictly for direction, then test whether a third variable or reverse causation explains the relationship when no random assignment occurred.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Operational Definition, Random Assignment, and Confounding Confusion
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners conflate random selection (generalizing to a population) with random assignment (controlling preexisting group differences), accept vague constructs as operational definitions, or miss placebo and experimenter-expectancy confounds.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify four research pillars in order: exact measurable operational definition, independent variable manipulation, random assignment vs. random sampling, and blinding against expectancy bias.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Negative Reinforcement vs. Positive Punishment Reversal
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners read "negative" as "unpleasant punishment" instead of "subtraction of a stimulus", causing them to misclassify behaviors strengthened by removing an aversive cue as punishment.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Apply a strict 2×2 operant decision grid: first decide whether the target behavior increases (reinforcement) or decreases (punishment), then decide whether a stimulus is added (positive) or removed (negative).

misconceptionFamilies.label: Sensation vs. Perception and Bottom-Up vs. Top-Down Conflation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners blur physical receptor transduction (sensation) with cortical selection, grouping, and schema-guided interpretation (perception), or mislabel expectation-driven perceptual sets as bottom-up processing.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Locate the process on the sensory-to-cognitive pipeline: physical energy → receptor transduction (sensation/bottom-up) versus prior schemas, context, and expectations shaping meaning (perception/top-down).

misconceptionFamilies.label: Neurotransmitter and Brain-Localization Oversimplification
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners swap agonists with antagonists, confuse reuptake inhibitors with receptor blockers, or mix up paired neural structures such as Broca vs. Wernicke areas, hippocampus vs. amygdala, and sympathetic vs. parasympathetic branches.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify synaptic direction (increases vs. blocks signaling) and pair each neural structure with its signature clinical deficit rather than a vague one-word nickname.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Reliability vs. Validity and Biopsychosocial Attribution Trap
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners equate test consistency (reliability) with measuring the intended construct (validity), or reduce psychological disorders and health outcomes to a single isolated biological or environmental cause.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Separate consistency across trials (reliability) from construct accuracy (validity), and map clinical/health scenarios across all three interacting biopsychosocial domains before choosing an explanation or intervention.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Correlation vs. Causation and Third-Variable Blindness
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Reading Correlation Strength, Direction, and Third-Variable Limits
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You concluded that variable A causes variable B from a survey or naturalistic observation, or ranked r = +0.35 as stronger than r = −0.78.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which value has the larger distance from zero (|r|), and what unmeasured third variable could simultaneously drive both measured variables?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the study method in the missed item for manipulation and random assignment; if both are absent, flag every causal verb ("causes", "leads to", "prevents", "reduces") in the choices as an overclaim.
stages.requiredOutput: A quick audit stating study design (correlational vs. experimental), the sign/magnitude breakdown of r, and the flagged causal distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Sketch a 3-node triangle for the scenario showing A ↔ B along with a plausible third variable C (such as socioeconomic status, sleep deprivation, or baseline stress) pointing to both A and B.
stages.requiredOutput: A three-variable diagram plus one sentence explaining both reverse-directionality and third-variable alternatives.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Compare three correlation coefficients (r = −0.81, r = +0.52, r = −0.12) by predictive strength, then rewrite an overclaiming headline about screen time and anxiety into a defensible AP Psych conclusion.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct strength ranking (−0.81 strongest, −0.12 weakest) and a revised non-causal conclusion naming one plausible confounder.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed item and solve a fresh Unit 4 or Unit 5 study-critique item by confirming whether the conclusion matches the design limits.
stages.requiredOutput: Verified correct answers on both items with an explicit check of design-to-claim alignment.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Operational Definition, Random Assignment, and Confounding Confusion
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separating Operational Definitions, Random Assignment, and Sampling
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You answered that random assignment makes a sample representative of the population, or selected a broad conceptual label instead of a replicable measurement procedure as an operational definition.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this procedure determine WHO enters the study (random sampling → generalizability) or WHICH condition each participant receives (random assignment → causal control)?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify whether the missed item tested measurement precision (operational definition), external validity (random sampling), or internal validity (random assignment and double-blind control).
stages.requiredOutput: A one-line diagnosis naming the research-design concept targeted by the stem versus the concept confused in the chosen distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Convert the abstract psychological construct in the scenario (such as aggression, memory retention, or stress) into a concrete numeric operational definition, and pair random sampling with population generalization and random assignment with confounding control.
stages.requiredOutput: A replicable operational definition (with units or scoring criteria) plus a 2-row table separating random sampling from random assignment.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Critique a flawed memory experiment where morning volunteers receive mnemonic training and evening volunteers serve as the control group with an unblinded grader.
stages.requiredOutput: Identification of two confounds (time-of-day self-selection and experimenter bias) plus the exact design fixes (random assignment and double-blind scoring).

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the original research-methods item and one new Unit 2/4 experimental vignette, verifying both operational measurability and confound elimination.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct choices on both items accompanied by a brief justification naming the exact validity threat eliminated.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Negative Reinforcement vs. Positive Punishment Reversal
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Mastering the 2×2 Operant Conditioning Decision Matrix
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You labeled buckling a seatbelt to silence a car chime or taking aspirin to stop a headache as punishment because an unpleasant stimulus appeared in the story.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: After the consequence occurs, does the target behavior happen MORE often (reinforcement) or LESS often (punishment), and was a stimulus added (+) or removed (−)?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Isolate three elements in the missed Unit 3 scenario: the exact target behavior, whether its future frequency rises or falls, and whether the consequence adds or removes a stimulus.
stages.requiredOutput: A three-part breakdown exposing where emotional tone ("bad/unpleasant") hijacked the mathematical +/- and increase/decrease rule.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Fill in a 2×2 operant grid mapping Increase/Decrease on the rows and Add (+)/Remove (−) on the columns, placing the scenario cleanly in its single quadrant.
stages.requiredOutput: A completed 2×2 matrix with one concrete everyday example in each quadrant (PR, NR, PP, NP).

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Classify four quick AP Psych vignettes: ending a loud alarm by standing up (NR), losing phone privileges after curfew violation (NP), receiving extra chores after arguing (PP), and earning bonus credit for early submission (PR).
stages.requiredOutput: All four vignettes labeled accurately with explicit arrows showing behavior frequency direction and stimulus addition/removal.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed learning item and solve a paired classical-vs-operant item distinguishing voluntary consequence-driven learning from involuntary UCS → UCR / CS → CR associations.
stages.requiredOutput: Verified correct answers on both items without confusing negative reinforcement with punishment or classical conditioning.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Sensation vs. Perception and Bottom-Up vs. Top-Down Conflation
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separating Sensory Transduction from Schema-Driven Perception
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You called reading a misspelled sentence via context "bottom-up processing", or labeled retinal rod/cone transduction as "perception".
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the phenomenon happening at physical stimulus detection and neural transduction (sensation/bottom-up) or during brain-level interpretation guided by expectations and prior knowledge (perception/top-down)?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Trace the stimulus in the missed item from external energy to conscious meaning and pinpoint the boundary where receptor transduction ends and cortical interpretation begins.
stages.requiredOutput: A two-step pipeline note stating the sensory receptor involved and whether the item turns on transduction or cognitive expectation.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Contrast bottom-up feature assembly (receptors → feature detectors → whole object) against top-down guidance (perceptual set, priming, Gestalt context → expectation shaping what you notice).
stages.requiredOutput: A two-column comparison mapping key AP terms (absolute threshold, Weber law, transduction vs. perceptual set, figure-ground, binocular cues) to the right stage.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Classify two contrasting scenarios: a radiologist spotting a faint tumor cue using years of training (top-down perceptual set) versus a listener noticing a tone drop below their absolute threshold after sensory adaptation (sensation).
stages.requiredOutput: Two labeled justifications citing the exact cue (prior schema vs. receptor-level sensitivity shift).

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Unit 1/2 item and one unfamiliar Gestalt or selective-attention (inattentional blindness) item using the transduction-vs-interpretation check.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct choices on both items with a one-sentence confirmation of processing direction (bottom-up vs. top-down).

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Pinpointing Synaptic Drug Action and Paired Brain-Structure Deficits
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You labeled an SSRI reuptake inhibitor as an antagonist because it "blocks" a transporter, or swapped Broca expressive aphasia with Wernicke receptive aphasia.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this drug ultimately INCREASE postsynaptic neurotransmitter signaling (agonist) or DECREASE it (antagonist), and which exact functional deficit matches the damaged neural structure?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check the missed Unit 1 item to see whether the slip was a synaptic-direction inversion (blocking reuptake leaves MORE neurotransmitter in the cleft → agonist) or a swapped anatomical pair.
stages.requiredOutput: An exact error tag naming the confused neurotransmitter mechanism or brain-region pair.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Build a high-yield paired-contrast cheat sheet: agonist (mimics or blocks reuptake) vs. antagonist (blocks postsynaptic receptors); Broca (speech production, frontal) vs. Wernicke (language comprehension, temporal); hippocampus (explicit memory consolidation) vs. amygdala (fear/emotion).
stages.requiredOutput: A 4-pair clinical-deficit table linking each structure or synaptic mechanism to its unmistakable AP symptom signature.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Diagnose two short case vignettes: a stroke patient who speaks fluently in nonsensical sentences (Wernicke area) and a medication that binds to acetylcholine receptors without opening ion channels (ACh antagonist).
stages.requiredOutput: Correct diagnosis for both vignettes explaining the exact functional mechanism rather than a generic brain-lobe guess.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed neurobiology item and solve a fresh autonomic-nervous-system item contrasting sympathetic mobilization against parasympathetic recovery.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct answers on both items backed by precise synaptic or anatomical mechanism statements.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Reliability vs. Validity and Biopsychosocial Attribution Trap
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Distinguishing Test Consistency from Validity and Single-Cause Clinical Traps
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You judged a consistently biased scale as valid because scores repeated closely, or picked a purely biological or purely willpower explanation when the vignette included interacting biological, cognitive, and social stressors.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are the scores merely repeatable (reliable) or truly measuring the target construct (valid), and how do biological vulnerability, cognitive appraisal, and social context interact in this case?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Examine the missed Unit 5 item and highlight whether the distractor conflated test-retest/split-half consistency with construct/predictive validity, or ignored one of the three biopsychosocial legs.
stages.requiredOutput: A targeted error note distinguishing the psychometric property or clinical model factor missed in the original choice.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the bullseye rule (tight cluster off-center = reliable but invalid; centered tight cluster = reliable and valid) and map the clinical vignette onto a 3-column Biopsychosocial grid (Bio: genetics/neurochemistry; Psycho: maladaptive thoughts/coping; Social: support/culture/stressors).
stages.requiredOutput: A bullseye classification plus a filled 3-column biopsychosocial breakdown for the case.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Evaluate two items: a depression scale that yields identical scores every week yet mostly asks about math anxiety (high reliability, low construct validity) and a diathesis-stress depression vignette combining genetic vulnerability with job loss.
stages.requiredOutput: Two concise rationales demonstrating why reliability never guarantees validity and why diathesis-stress requires interaction rather than a single cause.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the original Unit 5 item and complete one therapy-matching transfer item pairing cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure, and biomedical interventions with their exact targets.
stages.requiredOutput: Verified correct answers on both items with explicit alignment to validity type or biopsychosocial mechanism.
